sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, press release Aug 1999, 'The Peregrine Falcon is Back!': world's fastest bird, reaching speeds of 200 miles an hour as it dives after its prey; DDT caused peregrines to lay thin-shelled eggs that broke during incubation; by 1975 an all-time low of 324 nesting pairs in North America; has adapted to nesting on skyscrapers where it hunts pigeons and starlings; https://www.fws.gov/press-release/1999-08/peregrine-falcon-back-babbit-announces-removal-worlds-fastest-bird-endangered

Cornell Lab of Ornithology, All About Birds, Peregrine Falcon: hunting stoop from heights of over 1 km, reaching about 320 km/h (200 mph); hunts medium-sized birds; nearly eradicated from eastern North America by pesticide poisoning, now regularly seen in large cities; found on every continent except Antarctica; https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Peregrine_Falcon/overview

BBC Wildlife (Discover Wildlife), Peregrine falcon facts: folds wings and tail into a teardrop shape and strikes prey in mid-air with its talons; the tomial tooth, a notch on the upper bill, breaks the prey's neck and spinal cord; tubercles in the nostrils slow incoming air so it can breathe while diving; a semi-transparent nictitating membrane protects the eyes at top speed; nests on high-rise blocks and cathedrals as replicas of its cliff ledges; feral pigeons are common urban prey; https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/birds/peregrine-falcon-facts
